query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, resistance to corrosion is enhanced when the material’s microstructure permits effective hydrogen out-diffusion; in contrast, pre-strain introduces dislocation trapping sites that retain hydrogen, disrupting the protective passive oxide layer and promoting localized corrosion and embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: Steel samples with an intact passive oxide layer and an un-prestrained microstructure (minimal dislocation density).
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled hydrogen charging (simulating operational hydrogen exposure) with simultaneous application of varying degrees of pre-strain on some specimens.
generation.conditions: Ambient and operational temperatures relevant to chemical processing and nuclear power plants; tests conducted under controlled hydrogen exposure followed by air exposure and then immersion in a corrosive media that simulates service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The density of dislocations and microstructural defects introduced by pre-strain that serve as hydrogen trapping sites.
generation.mechanism: In samples with unaltered microstructure, hydrogen absorbed during exposure diffuses out during air exposure, preserving the protective passive oxide film that resists corrosion. Pre-strained samples develop additional dislocation sites that trap hydrogen, leading to local embrittlement and degradation of the oxide film, which in turn promotes corrosion initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Un-prestrained samples will show low retained hydrogen levels, maintain a robust passive oxide film, and exhibit lower corrosion rates and higher fracture energy, whereas pre-strained samples will exhibit higher hydrogen retention, compromised oxide integrity, lower fracture energy, and accelerated corrosion.
generation.baseline: Steel samples that are neither pre-strained nor hydrogen-charged, which should display stable oxide layers, low hydrogen content, and predictable corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold primarily for carbon steels and low-alloy steels typical in chemical-processing and nuclear-power settings. It may not apply to high-alloy stainless steels where corrosion mechanisms are governed by different chemistry and passivation behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: It remains unclear whether these findings can be generalized across all steel grades and under the full range of operational stresses, particularly in environments where additional corrosive agents or inhibitors are present.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare paired sets of steel specimens. One set remains in an un-prestrained state while the other is subjected to controlled pre-straining to introduce dislocation sites. Expose both sets to identical hydrogen charging protocols followed by defined periods of air exposure to allow for hydrogen desorption. Finally, immerse samples in a simulated corrosive environment that mimics operational conditions. Compare the hydrogen content, oxide layer integrity, fracture energy, and overall corrosion rates between the two groups.
measurements: Hydrogen concentration using thermal desorption spectroscopy
Oxide film characteristics (thickness, morphology) using electron microscopy and surface analysis
Corrosion rate via weight loss measurements or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-strained samples do not exhibit significantly higher hydrogen retention, degraded oxide layer integrity, lower fracture energy, and increased corrosion rates compared to un-prestrained samples, then the hypothesis that pre-strain induced hydrogen trapping is the governing mechanism for reduced corrosion resistance would be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn the paper, experimental studies of the hydrogen and pre-strained effect on fracture resistance of steam generator steel 22K were carried out. Special cylindrical samples were loaded up to fracture under a uniaxial tensile test with different pre-strained degrees and hydrogen charged times of the material. Stress-strain curves «Si–ei» were plotted. The true strain «ei» in the local volume was determined using the method of optical-digital image correlation (ODIC). The results showed that the hydrogen influence is practically absent in the elastic area of strain. The fracture energy of steel 22K decreases under the hydrogen influence and pre-strain in all investigated cases. It is shown that during six months of air exposure, with the 0% pre-strained samples release almost all hydrogen. In pre-strained samples, the hydrogen concentration decreased by 1–3% compared to the initial values. This indicates that they have trapped hydrogen that cannot escape on its own. Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) indexes for 0% pre-strained samples at different levels of hydrogen-charging calculated by the strain and energy approaches are equal to each other.
